title: Binary Search Trees: Insert
oneLiner: Walk down comparing at each node -- smaller goes left, bigger or equal goes right -- until you find the empty spot this value belongs in.
keyTakeaway: A tree is made of nodes: the top one is the root, each node in a binary tree has up to two children (left and right), a node with no children is a leaf, and a node plus everything below it is a subtree. A binary search tree keeps one invariant (a rule that is always true) at every single node: everything in its LEFT subtree is smaller, everything in its RIGHT subtree is bigger or equal (these lessons send duplicates right). Insertion just walks that invariant downward -- compare, go left or right, repeat -- until it falls off the tree into an empty spot, which is exactly where the new value belongs.
explanation: Starting from the root, compare the value being inserted to the current node: smaller means "it belongs somewhere in the left subtree," so move to the left child and repeat the comparison there; bigger (or equal, by convention here) means move right instead. Eventually this walk reaches a node with no child on the side it needs to go -- that empty spot is exactly where the new value belongs, becoming a new leaf. Insert several values one at a time this way and the whole tree builds itself, always keeping the BST property (left < node <= right, with equal values going right, at every node, not just the root) intact. Watch out for what the ORDER of insertion does to the tree's shape: inserting already-sorted values one at a time (1, 2, 3, 4...) produces a tree that's really just a linked list leaning one direction -- every operation degrades to O(n) instead of the O(log n) a balanced tree (one whose left and right sides are about equally deep) gives you. (Keeping a BST balanced under insertion is a real algorithm in its own right -- AVL and red-black trees -- out of scope here, but worth knowing the plain version doesn't self-balance.)

visualizationSteps.message: Inserting [5, 3, 8, 1, 4] one at a time into an empty BST.
Insert 5: tree is empty -- 5 becomes the root.
Insert 3: 3 < 5, go left -- empty spot, place 3 here.
Insert 8: 8 >= 5, go right -- empty spot, place 8 here.
Insert 1: 1 < 3, go left -- empty spot, place 1 here.
Insert 4: 4 >= 3, go right -- empty spot, place 4 here.

complexity.note: BuildBst inserts all n values, and each insert walks one root-to-leaf path of the tree built so far, which costs at most its height h. That is O(n · h) in total: O(n log n) while the tree stays balanced, but O(n²) in the worst case, because sorted input turns the tree into a chain and the i-th insert walks i nodes. Space is O(n) for the n nodes of the tree, plus O(h) recursion stack for the recursive insert (O(1) iterative), and h is at most n.
